hook: The same model, on the same GPU, runs your prompt about fifty times faster than it writes the answer. Here is why.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — The same model, on the same GPU, reads your prompt about fifty times faster per token than it writes the answer. Here is why.

0:15 QUESTION — Every ChatGPT or Claude request has two phases. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one forward pass. Decode writes one token per pass. vLLM, SGLang and the featherserve engine we build in this module all schedule these two phases differently, so we need to see the difference with a stopwatch first.

1:00 INTUITION — Prefill is a matrix-matrix multiply: T prompt tokens share one read of the weights. Decode is a matrix-vector multiply: one token pays for the full weight read alone. Same weights, wildly different work per byte. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Forward FLOPs per token are about 2N for N params. Prefill of T tokens: 2NT FLOPs, reads 2N bytes of bf16 weights, so intensity is about T FLOP/byte. Decode at batch 1: 2N FLOPs, still reads 2N bytes, so intensity is about 1 FLOP/byte. Ridge point of a 4090 is 165e12 / 1.008e12, about 165 FLOP/byte. So prefill with T above roughly 165 is compute-bound, decode at batch 1 is memory-bound. Lower bound for one decode step on Qwen3-0.6B: 1.2 GB / 1008 GB/s, about 1.2 ms.

5:30 CODE — Load Qwen3-0.6B with transformers in bf16. Write time_prefill(model, input_ids) that runs one forward over the prompt with use_cache=True and returns elapsed time and past_key_values. Write time_decode(model, past, n=128) that feeds one token at a time. On Mac use time.perf_counter and torch.mps.synchronize; on CUDA use torch.cuda.Event with synchronize. Sweep prompt length 128, 512, 2048.

9:00 RECEIPT — Assert the greedy token from the prefill logits equals the first token of model.generate(input_ids, max_new_tokens=1, do_sample=False). Then print prefill tokens/s and decode tokens/s; expect prefill tokens/s to be one to two orders of magnitude higher.
10:30 MEASURE — Bar chart: ms per token for prefill vs decode at three prompt lengths. Overlay the 1.2 ms bandwidth floor for decode on the 4090 line if you have one.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Prefill is compute-bound, decode is memory-bound, and every inference trick in this module attacks one of the two. Interview line: TTFT is a prefill problem, TPOT is a bandwidth problem.
12:00 NEXT — Next: The KV cache from scratch
key_math: FLOPs_fwd ~ 2*N*T; bytes_weights = 2*N (bf16); intensity_prefill ~ T FLOP/byte; intensity_decode(batch B) ~ B FLOP/byte; ridge_4090 = 165e12/1.008e12 ~ 165 FLOP/byte; t_decode_min = bytes_weights / bandwidth
code_task: time_prefill(model, input_ids[1,T]) -> (seconds, past_key_values); time_decode(model, past, first_tok[1,1], n) -> seconds per token. Sweep T in {128,512,2048}; report tokens/s for each phase. Qwen3-0.6B bf16.
receipt: assert prefill_logits[0,-1].argmax().item() == model.generate(input_ids, max_new_tokens=1, do_sample=False)[0,-1].item(); then print(prefill_tok_s / decode_tok_s) and expect a ratio > 10 at T=2048.
gotchas: Timing without synchronize measures kernel launch, not compute; the first call includes warmup and allocator growth, so discard it; generate() hides both phases, so call the model forward directly.
interview_q: Why is LLM decode memory-bound but prefill compute-bound? Decode multiplies the weights by a single token vector, so each weight byte loaded does about one FLOP, far below the GPU ridge point. Prefill reuses each weight across T tokens, so intensity scales with T.
explainer: Here is one request split into two phases: a long prompt on the left, and the answer growing token by token on the right.
During prefill, all prompt tokens enter the model together, so the weight matrix multiplies a tall block of activations in one shot.
During decode, only one new token enters, so the same huge weight matrix multiplies a single thin vector.
We count the bytes: both phases stream every weight from memory once, about two bytes per parameter in bf16.
But prefill does T times more math per byte loaded, so its dot climbs the roofline into the compute-bound region.
Decode's dot sits far left at about one FLOP per byte, pinned under the slanted memory bandwidth line.
That is why the stopwatch shows prefill tokens flying by while decode tokens drip out one at a time.
explainer_visuals: Timeline bar: blue prefill block of 2048 tokens, then orange decode ticks one per step.
Weight matrix W (d x d) times activation block X (T x d), highlighted as one big GEMM.
Same W times a single row vector x (1 x d), GEMV, mostly empty compute grid.
Bytes counter: 2N bytes streaming from HBM bar into SM boxes, identical for both.
Roofline plot log-log; prefill dot at intensity T=2048 sitting on the flat compute roof.
Decode dot at intensity 1 on the bandwidth slope, ridge marked at 165 FLOP/byte.
Two stopwatches side by side: prefill tokens/s large number, decode tokens/s small number.
short: The MATH beat: 'Your GPU reads prompts 50x faster than it writes answers.' Caption: 'Prefill vs decode in one roofline.'

The roofline explains it exactly: decode does about one FLOP per weight byte, so it is a bandwidth problem, not a compute problem.

hook: Without a KV cache, generating 1000 tokens redoes about 500,000 token computations. With it, 1000. One dictionary fixes that.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Without a KV cache, generating a thousand tokens recomputes about half a million token positions. With it, a thousand. One tensor buffer fixes that.

0:15 QUESTION — Every production engine, vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, is built around the KV cache. It is the single data structure that featherserve will spend most of its memory and code managing, so we build it by hand on our own GPT first.

1:00 INTUITION — Causal attention means old tokens never change their keys and values when new tokens arrive. So computing them again is pure waste. Keep them in a buffer, append one row per step. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Step t needs q_t K_{1:t}^T and the weighted sum over V_{1:t}. K_{1:t} = [K_{1:t-1}; k_t], so we only compute k_t, v_t. Cost without cache, summed over n steps: sum_t t ~ n^2/2 token forwards. With cache: n token forwards plus attention reads of t rows. Memory cost: KV bytes per token = 2 * L * n_kv * d_head * bytes. Qwen3-0.6B: 2 * 28 * 8 * 128 * 2 = 114,688 bytes, 112 KiB per token. A 32k context is 3.5 GiB for one sequence.

5:00 CODE — In our M05 GPT, add class KVCache with k, v tensors of shape [L, B, n_kv, max_len, d_head] and a pos counter. In attention: compute q,k,v for the new tokens only, write k,v into cache[layer, :, :, pos:pos+T], then call F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k_cache[..., :pos+T, :], v_cache[..., :pos+T, :], is_causal=(T>1)). Apply RoPE with position offset pos before writing k. generate_cached(model, prompt, n) does one prefill then a decode loop.

8:30 RECEIPT — Greedy decode 200 tokens with and without cache: assert torch.equal(gen_nocache, gen_cached). Second check on Qwen3-0.6B: compare our cached logits to HF model(input_ids, past_key_values=...) with torch.testing.assert_close(atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2) in bf16.
10:00 MEASURE — Plot ms per generated token vs position for both versions. No-cache grows linearly; cached stays nearly flat. Report end-to-end speedup at 512 tokens.

11:00 TAKEAWAY — The KV cache trades memory for compute, and that memory becomes the thing the whole engine schedules around. Interview line: compute KV bytes per token as 2 times layers times KV heads times head dim times bytes.
11:30 NEXT — Next: Why decode is memory-bound
key_math: K_{1:t} = concat(K_{1:t-1}, k_t); cost_nocache ~ sum_{t=1}^n t = n(n+1)/2; KV_bytes_per_token = 2 * L * n_kv * d_head * bytes; Qwen3-0.6B = 2*28*8*128*2 = 114,688 B
code_task: class KVCache: k,v [L,B,n_kv,max_len,d_head], pos:int, update(layer, k_new[B,n_kv,T,d_head], v_new) -> (k_all, v_all). Attention.forward(x[B,T,d], cache, layer) with RoPE offset. generate_cached(model, idx[B,T0], max_new) -> idx[B,T0+max_new].
receipt: assert torch.equal(generate_nocache(m, p, 200), generate_cached(m, p, 200)); for Qwen3-0.6B, torch.testing.assert_close(my_logits, hf_logits, atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2).
gotchas: Forgetting the RoPE position offset gives right shapes and wrong text; is_causal=True on a single query token with a longer key masks everything except the first key, so use is_causal only for the prefill; with GQA, repeat or broadcast KV heads at attention time, never store them repeated.
interview_q: How much KV cache does Llama-3-8B need for a 128k context in bf16? 2 * 32 layers * 8 KV heads * 128 * 2 bytes = 128 KiB per token, so 128k tokens is 16 GiB for a single sequence, more than the weights.
explainer: Here is the attention matrix for a growing sequence, one new row of queries added at each decode step.
Without a cache, every step recomputes keys and values for the entire prefix, the whole grey triangle again.
But causal masking means a past token's key and value never change when future tokens arrive.
So we store them in a buffer, and each step only computes one new key row and one new value row.
The new query attends over the cached keys, a single row of scores instead of a whole matrix.
The price is memory: two tensors per layer per token, which we total up for Qwen3 at 112 kibibytes.
Multiply by context length and batch, and the cache, not the weights, becomes the thing we must manage.
explainer_visuals: Lower-triangular attention heatmap growing one row per frame.
Entire triangle flashing grey on each step labelled recompute.
Past K and V columns locked with a padlock icon.
KV buffer as a long strip; one new orange slot appended per step.
Single query row q_t dotted against stacked K rows, producing one score vector.
Counter: 2 x 28 x 8 x 128 x 2 B = 112 KiB, per token.
Bar chart: weights 1.2 GB vs KV cache at 32k context 3.5 GiB, cache bar taller.
short: The MEASURE beat: flat vs rising ms-per-token lines. Caption: 'One buffer, O(n^2) to O(n).'
yt_title: KV Cache from Scratch in PyTorch: token-identical and 10x faster
x_post: Built a KV cache into my GPT from scratch. Greedy output is token-identical to the uncached model, and per-token latency goes flat. The catch: Qwen3-0.6B needs 112 KiB per token, so 32k context is 3.5 GiB. Memory is the new bottleneck. Code + video:
linkedin: Implemented a KV cache from scratch and verified generation is token-identical to the uncached path. Per-token latency went from linear in position to nearly flat. The real lesson is the memory bill: 112 KiB per token for Qwen3-0.6B, which is what the rest of featherserve has to manage.

hook: Doubling the batch size makes decode almost free, right up until it suddenly does not. The knee is a number you can compute.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Doubling the decode batch is almost free, right up until it is not. The knee is a number you can compute before you run anything.

0:15 QUESTION — Why does every serving system obsess over batch size? Because at batch 1, a 4090 running Qwen3-1.7B uses well under one percent of its tensor cores. Batching is the only way to buy back that compute, and featherserve's scheduler exists to keep batches big.

1:00 INTUITION — Reading the weights is a fixed toll per step. Each extra sequence in the batch rides along on the same read, adding a little math and its own KV cache read. Throughput rises linearly until compute or KV bandwidth catches up. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Per decode step at batch B: FLOPs ~ 2NB; bytes ~ 2N (weights) + B * S * kv_bytes_per_token (each sequence reads its cache of length S). Weight-only intensity = 2NB / 2N = B. Ridge on 4090 ~165, so weights stop dominating around B ~ 165. Step time ~ max(2NB / 165e12, (2N + B*S*kv) / 1.008e12). For Qwen3-1.7B (about 3.4 GB bf16 weights, 112 KiB per token) at S=1024, each sequence adds 0.11 GiB of KV reads, so KV traffic overtakes weight traffic near B ~ 30. That is the real knee for long contexts.

5:00 CODE — Write bench_decode(model, B, S, steps=50): build a random prefix of length S for B sequences, prefill once, then time 50 decode steps with CUDA events. Sweep B in 1,2,4,...,256. Write predict_step_time(N, B, S, kv_bytes, bw=1.008e12, flops=165e12) implementing the max() model. Plot measured vs predicted.
8:30 RECEIPT — At B=1, assert measured step time is within 1.5x of the bandwidth floor 2N/1.008e12, about 3.4 ms. Print achieved bandwidth = bytes / time; expect 70 to 90 percent of 1008 GB/s.
10:00 MEASURE — Two plots: tokens/s vs batch (log x) with the linear region and knee, and achieved GB/s vs batch. Repeat at S=128 and S=2048 to show the knee move left as contexts grow.
11:30 TAKEAWAY — Decode throughput is bought with batch size, and the KV cache is what eventually pays the bill. Interview line: the decode roofline intensity is roughly the batch size.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Inference metrics
key_math: intensity_decode ~ 2NB / 2N = B; t_step ~ max(2NB / F_peak, (2N + B*S*kv_bytes) / BW); 4090: F_peak ~ 165e12, BW ~ 1.008e12 B/s; knee where B*S*kv_bytes ~ 2N
code_task: bench_decode(model, B:int, S:int, steps:int) -> (ms_per_step, tokens_per_s); predict_step_time(N, B, S, kv_bytes, bw, flops) -> seconds. Sweep B in powers of 2 up to 256 for S in {128,1024,2048}. Qwen3-1.7B bf16 on RTX 4090.
receipt: assert measured_ms(B=1) < 1.5 * (2*N / 1.008e12 * 1e3); print achieved_GBps = (2*N + B*S*kv_bytes) / t; expect 700-900 GB/s at small B.
gotchas: HF generate pads and adds overhead, so drive forward() with a static KV buffer; OOM at large B and S because KV grows as B*S, so compute memory before launching; Python launch overhead dominates tiny models at B=1, which looks like a slow GPU but is the CPU (fixed in M13E12).
interview_q: Why does increasing batch size improve decode throughput almost linearly at first? Each step streams all weights once regardless of batch, so extra sequences reuse the same bytes; intensity grows with B until compute or per-sequence KV reads become the bottleneck.
explainer: Here is the roofline again, and we place one decode dot for each batch size from one to two hundred fifty six.
At batch one the dot sits far down the bandwidth slope, doing about one FLOP for every weight byte.
Each doubling of the batch slides the dot right, and throughput doubles because the weight read is shared.
But every sequence also drags its own KV cache through memory, a cost that grows with batch and context.
We stack the two byte costs as bars: fixed weight bytes in blue, growing KV bytes in orange.
Where the orange bar overtakes the blue, the free lunch ends and the curve bends over.
Longer contexts make the orange bar grow faster, so the knee moves to smaller batches.
explainer_visuals: Log-log roofline with ridge at 165 FLOP/byte marked.
Single dot at x=1 on the bandwidth line.
Dots at 2,4,8,...,128 sliding right, tokens/s labels doubling.
Each sequence drawn as a strip of KV blocks feeding into the memory pipe.
Stacked bar chart per batch size: blue constant weights, orange KV bytes rising.
Measured tokens/s curve bending at the crossover, knee annotated.
Three curves for S=128, 1024, 2048 with knees moving left.
short: The INTUITION beat: 'Batching is free until the KV cache sends the bill.' Caption: 'Decode throughput vs batch size on a 4090.'
yt_title: Why LLM Decode Is Memory-Bound: batch size vs throughput on a 4090
x_post: Decode intensity is roughly your batch size in FLOP/byte. A 4090's ridge is ~165. So batch 1 wastes over 99% of the tensor cores. Measured the curve on Qwen3-1.7B and the knee lands where KV reads overtake weight reads. Code + video:
linkedin: Measured decode throughput vs batch size for Qwen3-1.7B on an RTX 4090 and fit it with a two-term bandwidth model. At batch 1 the GPU hit close to its 1 TB/s bandwidth floor while using a tiny fraction of its compute. The knee is set by KV cache traffic, which is why continuous batching and paged memory come next.

hook: Your server can double its throughput and get worse for users. That is why serious teams measure goodput, not tokens per second.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Your server can double its throughput and get worse for every user. That is why serious teams measure goodput, not tokens per second.

0:15 QUESTION — When vLLM or SGLang publish a benchmark, they report TTFT, inter-token latency and throughput at a request rate. If featherserve is going to be compared to them honestly, our load generator has to measure the same things the same way.

1:00 INTUITION — A user feels two delays: how long until the first word appears, and how smoothly the rest streams. The operator feels one number: how many requests per second the GPU clears. Goodput is the rate of requests that meet both user SLOs. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Per request: TTFT = t_first_token - t_send. E2E = t_last - t_send. TPOT = (E2E - TTFT) / (n_out - 1). ITL_i = t_{i+1} - t_i for each streamed token, so mean ITL approximates TPOT but its p99 catches stalls. Throughput = total output tokens / wall time. Goodput = requests per second with TTFT <= SLO_ttft and TPOT <= SLO_tpot. Arrivals: Poisson with rate lambda, so inter-arrival gaps are Exponential(lambda), sampled as -ln(U)/lambda. Report p50, p90, p99, never just the mean.

5:00 CODE — Write an asyncio load generator: async def send(session, prompt, max_tokens) posts to /v1/completions with stream=True via aiohttp and records a timestamp per SSE chunk. async def run(rate, n, dataset) launches requests with exponential gaps. def summarize(records, slo_ttft=0.5, slo_tpot=0.05) returns a dict of percentiles, throughput and goodput. Point it at a local vLLM server: vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B.

8:30 RECEIPT — Run vllm bench serve against the same server with --dataset-name random, matching --random-input-len, --random-output-len, --num-prompts and --request-rate. Assert our median TTFT and mean TPOT are within 10 percent of vLLM's reported numbers.
10:00 MEASURE — Sweep request rate from 1 to 32 req/s. Plot throughput and goodput on the same axis: throughput keeps rising, goodput peaks and falls once p99 TTFT blows the SLO.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Throughput is what the GPU does, goodput is what users get, and you must report latency percentiles at a stated request rate. Interview line: always name the SLO before quoting a throughput number.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Static vs continuous batching
key_math: TTFT = t_1 - t_send; TPOT = (t_last - t_1) / (n_out - 1); ITL_i = t_{i+1} - t_i; goodput = |{r : TTFT_r <= S_ttft and TPOT_r <= S_tpot}| / T_wall; Poisson gaps dt = -ln(U)/lambda
code_task: Async load generator: send(session, prompt, max_tokens) -> {t_send, t_tokens:list[float], n_out}; run(rate:float, n:int, prompts) -> list[records]; summarize(records, slo_ttft, slo_tpot) -> dict(p50/p90/p99 TTFT, TPOT, ITL, throughput_tok_s, goodput_req_s). Targets any OpenAI-compatible server, later featherserve.
receipt: Our median TTFT and mean TPOT on vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B match `vllm bench serve --dataset-name random` at the same --request-rate within 10%.
gotchas: SSE chunks can carry several tokens, so count tokens from usage or the tokenizer, not chunks; a closed-loop client (send next after previous finishes) hides queueing, use open-loop Poisson arrivals; warm the server first or the first requests include CUDA graph capture and compile.
interview_q: What is the difference between TPOT and ITL, and why report p99? TPOT averages decode time per output token for a request; ITL is each individual gap, so its tail exposes stalls such as a long prefill blocking decodes. Users feel the tail, so p99 matters more than the mean.
explainer: Here is one streaming request on a timeline, from the moment it is sent to its final token.
The first gap, until the first token arrives, is time to first token, mostly queueing plus prefill.
Each following gap between tokens is an inter-token latency, and their average is time per output token.
Now we fire many requests with random Poisson arrivals, each one its own row of tick marks.
As the request rate rises, queues form inside the server, and the first-token gaps start stretching out row by row.
We colour each request green if it met both latency targets, red if it missed either one.
Throughput counts every token, but goodput counts only the green requests, so its curve peaks earlier and then falls.

Bracket labelled TTFT from send to first tick.
Small brackets between ticks labelled ITL, average line labelled TPOT.
Stacked timelines of 20 requests with exponential arrival offsets.
TTFT brackets lengthening as density of arrivals increases.
Same rows recoloured green and red against SLO thresholds.
Plot of throughput (rising) and goodput (peaking then falling) vs request rate.
short: The MEASURE beat: throughput rises, goodput collapses. Caption: 'More tokens per second, worse service.'
yt_title: LLM Inference Metrics: TTFT, TPOT, ITL and goodput, measured
x_post: Built an async load generator for LLM servers. Throughput kept climbing with request rate, but goodput (requests meeting TTFT and TPOT SLOs) peaked and crashed. Numbers match vllm bench serve within 10%. Code + video:
linkedin: Wrote a Poisson-arrival load generator that reports TTFT, TPOT, ITL percentiles and goodput for any OpenAI-compatible server, and validated it against vllm bench serve. The striking result: past a certain request rate, throughput rises while goodput falls. This harness is how featherserve will be judged.

hook: Static batching makes a two-word answer wait for a two-thousand-word answer. Orca fixed it by scheduling every single step.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Static batching makes a two-word answer wait for a two-thousand-word essay. Orca fixed that by rescheduling the batch at every single step.

0:15 QUESTION — The Orca paper reported 36.9x throughput over FasterTransformer on GPT-3 175B at the same latency. Every modern engine, vLLM, SGLang, TGI, uses its idea. This is featherserve's first real component: the scheduler.

1:00 INTUITION — Static batching is a bus that leaves when full and waits until the last passenger gets off. Continuous batching is a train that stops every station: finished sequences leave, waiting ones board, at every decode iteration. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Static batch wasted slots: for output lengths l_i, the batch runs max_i l_i steps, so utilization = sum_i l_i / (B * max_i l_i). With lengths uniform on [1, 1000], expected utilization is about 50 percent, worse with long tails. Continuous batching keeps the batch full whenever the queue is non-empty, so utilization approaches 1 minus scheduling overhead. Admission constraint: sum over running sequences of (prompt_len + generated) * kv_bytes <= KV budget.

4:30 CODE — Write class Sequence (id, token_ids, prompt_len, max_tokens, status in WAITING, RUNNING, FINISHED). class Scheduler with waiting deque and running list; step() admits from waiting while KV budget allows, then returns a batch: new sequences need prefill, running ones need one decode token. For now run prefill per new sequence and decode as one batched forward with left-padded or per-sequence caches. engine_step() calls model, samples, appends tokens, retires sequences on EOS or max_tokens. Compare against static_generate that batches B prompts and runs to the longest.

8:30 RECEIPT — Correctness: for 64 prompts with greedy sampling, assert every sequence's output from the continuous scheduler equals its output when run alone. Performance: on a workload with output lengths sampled from a long-tailed distribution, print slot utilization; expect static near 30 to 50 percent and continuous above 90 percent.

10:00 MEASURE — Using last episode's load generator, plot throughput and p50 latency vs request rate for static vs continuous batching on Qwen3-0.6B. Compare the ratio to Orca's reported gains and explain why ours is smaller on one GPU.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Schedule at the granularity of iterations, not requests, and the GPU never waits for the slowest sequence. Interview line: Orca's two ideas are iteration-level scheduling and selective batching.
12:00 NEXT — Next: PagedAttention
key_math: util_static = sum_i l_i / (B * max_i l_i); E[util] for l ~ U[1,L] with large B -> ~1/2; KV admission: sum_{s in running} (p_s + g_s) * kv_bytes_per_token <= M_kv
code_task: Sequence(id, token_ids, prompt_len, max_tokens, status); Scheduler(max_batch, kv_budget_tokens).add(seq), .step() -> (prefill_seqs, decode_seqs); Engine.step() runs model and appends sampled tokens; static_generate(prompts, B) baseline. Qwen3-0.6B, greedy.
receipt: for s in seqs: assert cont_outputs[s.id] == solo_outputs[s.id] (greedy, token-identical); util_continuous > 0.9 and util_static < 0.5 on the long-tail workload.
gotchas: Left padding without fixing position ids and attention masks silently corrupts outputs, which the solo-equality check catches; retiring sequences while iterating the running list skips one, iterate over a copy; admitting until memory runs out mid-generation causes OOM, so reserve KV for max_tokens or implement preemption.
interview_q: Why does continuous batching help more when output lengths vary a lot? Static batching runs for the longest sequence, so short requests leave idle slots; iteration-level scheduling refills those slots every step, keeping effective batch size and throughput high.
explainer: Here are eight requests in a static batch, drawn as rows whose lengths are their output token counts.
The batch runs until the longest row finishes, so the grey area after short rows is wasted GPU time.
Meanwhile new requests pile up in a waiting queue on the right, unable to board.
Continuous batching checks the batch after every single decode step, instead of waiting until the whole batch is finished.
When a row finishes, its slot is immediately filled by the next waiting request, which runs its prefill.
The grid now stays almost fully coloured, and the waiting queue on the right drains steadily instead of piling up.
The only rule is memory: we admit a new request only if its KV cache fits in the budget.
explainer_visuals: Grid: 8 rows x time columns, coloured cells per generated token, varying row lengths.
Grey shaded region to the right of short rows, labelled wasted slots.
Queue of request boxes stacking up.
Clock tick marker sweeping one column at a time.
Finished row slot recoloured with a new request, prefill cell drawn wide.
Dense grid with utilization counter climbing to 95 percent.
KV budget bar filling; a request blocked when the bar would overflow.
short: The INTUITION beat: bus vs train animation. Caption: 'Continuous batching in 50 seconds.'
yt_title: Continuous Batching from Scratch: the Orca scheduler explained
x_post: Static batching waits for the longest sequence. Continuous batching (Orca) reschedules every decode step. My scheduler took slot utilization from under 50% to over 90% with token-identical outputs. First component of featherserve. Code + video:
linkedin: Built an iteration-level scheduler for my inference engine, featherserve, following Orca. Outputs stay token-identical to running each request alone, while slot utilization rose from under 50 percent to over 90 percent on a long-tailed workload. The constraint that remains is KV memory, which PagedAttention fixes next.

hook: Before vLLM, servers wasted 60 to 80 percent of their KV cache memory. The fix was invented for operating systems in the 1960s.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Before vLLM, servers wasted 60 to 80 percent of their KV cache memory. The fix was invented for operating systems decades ago.

0:15 QUESTION — The vLLM paper measured existing systems wasting most of their KV memory to fragmentation and over-reservation, and got waste under 4 percent with paging, for 2 to 4x throughput. This is the core of vLLM, nano-vllm, and now featherserve.

1:00 INTUITION — Contiguous KV buffers must reserve max length up front, like booking a whole hotel floor in case friends show up. Paging stores the cache in fixed-size blocks anywhere in a pool, and a block table maps logical positions to physical blocks, exactly like virtual memory. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Block size b tokens. Token at position t of a sequence lives in physical block block_table[t // b] at offset t % b. Pool size: n_blocks = floor(KV_budget / (b * kv_bytes_per_token)). Waste per sequence is at most b - 1 slots in its last block, so expected internal fragmentation is about (b-1)/2 tokens per sequence. For a 4090 with 12 GiB for KV and Qwen3-1.7B at 112 KiB per token, that is about 112k tokens, or 7,000 blocks of 16. Copy-on-write: shared prefix blocks keep a ref count and are copied only when written.

5:00 CODE — Write class BlockManager(num_blocks, block_size) with free list, ref_count, allocate(seq), append_slot(seq) returning a new block when t % b == 0, free(seq). Store K and V pools as tensors [L, num_blocks, block_size, n_kv, d_head]. Write paged_attention_ref(q[B,H,d], k_pool, v_pool, block_tables[B,max_blocks], seq_lens[B]) that gathers blocks with index_select, reshapes to contiguous K,V, masks past seq_len, and calls SDPA. Then a Triton or plain gather kernel optional. Plug into the scheduler: admission now checks free blocks, not reserved max length.

8:30 RECEIPT — Random block tables, random seq_lens up to 1000: torch.testing.assert_close(paged_attention_ref(q, k_pool, v_pool, bt, lens), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, K_dense, V_dense) with a length mask, atol=2e-3, rtol=2e-3) in bf16. End to end: greedy outputs identical to the contiguous-cache engine.

10:00 MEASURE — Max concurrent sequences before OOM on a 4090: contiguous reservation at max_len=8192 vs paged. Report KV memory utilization (used tokens / allocated tokens) for both; expect paged above 95 percent.
11:30 TAKEAWAY — Paging turns the KV cache from reserved arrays into an allocator, and that is what lets batch size grow. Interview line: fragmentation is bounded by one block per sequence.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Prefix caching and RadixAttention

KV pools [L, num_blocks, block_size, n_kv, d_head]. paged_attention_ref(q[B,H,d], k_pool, v_pool, block_tables[B,max_blocks] int32, seq_lens[B]) -> out[B,H,d]. Integrated into featherserve's scheduler.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(paged_attention_ref(q, kp, vp, bt, lens), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, K_dense, V_dense, attn_mask=len_mask), atol=2e-3, rtol=2e-3); greedy outputs equal the contiguous-cache engine token for token.
gotchas: Off-by-one when t % b == 0 either skips or double-allocates a block; padded entries in block_tables pointing at block 0 leak garbage unless masked by seq_len; GQA head mapping in the gather (query head h uses KV head h // (H / n_kv)).
interview_q: How does PagedAttention reduce KV memory waste? It allocates the cache in fixed-size blocks on demand and maps them through per-sequence block tables, so there is no max-length reservation and waste is at most one partial block per sequence; blocks can also be shared across sequences with copy-on-write.
explainer: Here is GPU memory with three sequences each given one contiguous slab reserved for the maximum length.
Most of each slab is empty, reserved for tokens that may never be generated, and gaps between slabs are unusable.
Paging cuts memory into small fixed blocks, each holding the keys and values for sixteen tokens.
Each sequence gets a block table, a short list mapping its logical blocks to physical blocks anywhere in the pool.
When a sequence fills its last block, the allocator hands it one more block from the free list.
Attention follows the block table, gathering scattered blocks as if they were one contiguous cache.
Waste shrinks to the unfilled tail of each last block, so far more sequences fit at once.

hook: Most requests to a chatbot start with the same system prompt. Recomputing it every time is the most expensive copy-paste in AI.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Most chatbot requests start with the same thousand-token system prompt. Recomputing it every time is the most expensive copy-paste in AI.

0:15 QUESTION — SGLang's RadixAttention reported up to 6.4x throughput on workloads with shared prefixes: few-shot prompts, multi-turn chat, agents, tree search. Anthropic and OpenAI both sell prompt caching as a product feature. featherserve needs it too.

1:00 INTUITION — Store every computed KV block in a tree keyed by tokens. A new request walks down the tree as far as its prefix matches and reuses those KV entries for free; only the unmatched suffix needs prefill. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — A radix tree compresses chains of single-child nodes into edges labelled with token sequences. Match cost is O(prompt length). Prefill saved per request = matched_len / prompt_len. Cache hit rate = sum matched tokens / sum prompt tokens. Eviction: each node has a ref count of running requests using it; only leaves with ref count 0 are evictable, in LRU order, so a shared prefix is never evicted while any request depends on it. Contrast with vLLM and nano-vllm: hash each full block by (parent hash, block tokens) and look it up in a dict; equivalent reuse at block granularity.

5:00 CODE — Write class RadixNode(children: dict[int, RadixNode], key: list[int], kv_indices: list[int], ref: int, last_access: float). class RadixCache with match_prefix(tokens) -> (node, matched_len, kv_indices), insert(tokens, kv_indices) with edge splitting, inc_ref/dec_ref along the path, evict(n_tokens) popping LRU zero-ref leaves from a heap. Wire into the scheduler: on admission, match, prefill only the suffix, insert on finish.

8:30 RECEIPT — Correctness: greedy outputs with the radix cache on equal outputs with it off, for 100 requests sharing a 1,000-token system prompt. Unit test: insert 'abcd', insert 'abxy', assert the root has one child with key 'ab' and two grandchildren. Hit rate on the shared-prompt workload should approach (1000) / (1000 + mean suffix).

10:00 MEASURE — Plot TTFT p50 vs number of requests with and without the cache. Then launch SGLang with and without --disable-radix-cache on the same workload and compare its hit-rate speedup to ours.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Prefix caching turns repeated context into a lookup, and a radix tree with ref-counted LRU eviction does it safely. Interview line: RadixAttention evicts leaves only, so shared prefixes survive.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Chunked prefill and scheduling policies
key_math: hit_rate = sum_r matched_r / sum_r prompt_len_r; prefill_tokens_r = prompt_len_r - matched_r; evictable = {leaf n : ref(n) = 0}, evict argmin last_access; block hash h_i = H(h_{i-1}, tokens_block_i)
code_task: RadixNode(children, key:list[int], kv_indices:list[int], ref:int, last_access); RadixCache.match_prefix(tokens) -> (node, n_matched, kv_idx), insert(tokens, kv_idx), inc_ref(node), dec_ref(node), evict(n_tokens). Plugged into featherserve's paged KV pool.
receipt: Outputs with cache == outputs without cache (greedy, 100 shared-prefix requests); tree-structure unit test after edge split; hit_rate within 2% of 1000/(1000+mean_suffix_len).
gotchas: Splitting an edge must split kv_indices at the same offset or KV gets misattributed; forgetting dec_ref on finish makes everything unevictable and memory leaks; the last prompt token must always be recomputed to produce logits, so cap matched_len at prompt_len - 1.
interview_q: How would you implement prompt caching in an inference server? Index computed KV by token prefix, either a radix tree like SGLang or chained block hashes like vLLM, reuse matched KV on admission, and evict unreferenced entries in LRU order, keeping shared prefixes pinned while in use.
explainer: Here are three requests that share the same long system prompt, with different user questions at the end.
Without caching, each one recomputes the same prefix, three identical blue bars of prefill work.
We insert the first request's tokens into a tree, one edge holding the whole shared prefix.
The second request walks down that edge, matches it, and branches off only where its question differs.
Matched tokens point straight at existing KV blocks, so only the short orange suffix is prefilled.
Each node counts how many running requests use it, and only unused leaves can be evicted.
The shared trunk stays warm while leaves churn, so hit rate climbs toward the prefix fraction.

hook: One user pastes a 30,000-token document, and every other user's stream freezes. Chunked prefill is the fix.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — One user pastes a thirty-thousand-token document, and every other user's stream freezes. Chunked prefill is the fix.

0:15 QUESTION — Our scheduler runs a new request's whole prefill in one step, so every decoding sequence waits for it. That shows up as giant ITL spikes. vLLM and SGLang both split long prefills into chunks and mix them with decodes. After this episode featherserve's core is complete, and project P2 starts.

1:00 INTUITION — Give each engine step a fixed token budget. Decodes go in first, one token each. The remaining budget is filled with a slice of a waiting prompt. Long prompts take several steps, but no step ever takes too long. Decodes are memory-bound and prefill is compute-bound, so mixing them uses both. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Token budget C per step (for example 512 or 2048). Step tokens = n_decode + chunk, with chunk = min(C - n_decode, remaining_prompt). Step time ~ max(compute(chunk + n_decode), bytes(weights + KV)) so adding a prefill chunk to a decode batch is nearly free until it crosses the compute ridge. A prompt of length P finishes prefill in ceil(P / (C - n_decode)) steps, so TTFT rises slightly while worst-case ITL is bounded by the time of a C-token step. Policies: FCFS for fairness, longest-prefix-match (SGLang's lpm) to maximize cache hits, and preemption by recompute or swap when blocks run out.

5:00 CODE — Extend Sequence with num_computed_tokens. Scheduler.step(budget) builds a batch: all running decodes first, then chunks of waiting prompts. The model runner takes a flat token batch with per-sequence (start, length) and positions, using the paged attention reference with causal masking inside each chunk against the cached prefix. Add policy='fcfs' or 'lpm' (sort waiting by radix match length). Add preemption: if append_slot fails, evict the newest running sequence and requeue it.

8:30 RECEIPT — Greedy outputs identical with chunk sizes 64, 512 and unlimited. Workload: 32 short chats decoding while a 16k-token prompt arrives; assert p99 ITL with chunking is below 2x the median ITL, while without chunking it spikes by an order of magnitude. Cross-check with SGLang: launch with --chunked-prefill-size at two values and compare its ITL tail.

10:00 MEASURE — Plot ITL over time for the decoding chats as the long prompt lands: a single tall spike without chunking, a band of small bumps with it. Table: chunk size vs TTFT of the long request vs p99 ITL of the others.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Chunked prefill trades a little TTFT for bounded inter-token latency, and the token budget is the knob. Interview line: mix compute-bound prefill chunks with memory-bound decodes to fill both rooflines.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Speculative decoding
key_math: chunk = min(C - n_decode, P - computed); steps_to_prefill = ceil(P / (C - n_decode)); t_step ~ max((2N*(chunk+n_decode))/F, (2N + KV_read)/BW); ITL_max ~ t_step(C)
code_task: Scheduler.step(token_budget:int, policy in {'fcfs','lpm'}) -> Batch(seq_ids, token_ids_flat, positions, query_start_loc, seq_lens); Sequence.num_computed_tokens; preempt(seq) by recompute. Model runner consumes flat varlen batches against paged KV.
receipt: Outputs identical for chunk in {64, 512, inf}; p99_ITL(chunked) < 2 * median_ITL while p99_ITL(unchunked) > 10 * median_ITL on the 16k-prompt interference workload.
gotchas: Only the final chunk of a prompt should be sampled from, earlier chunks produce no output token; causal mask inside a chunk must be offset by already-cached tokens; preempted sequences must release their blocks and radix refs or memory leaks.
interview_q: What problem does chunked prefill solve and what does it cost? It stops a long prompt from monopolizing a step and stalling every decode, bounding inter-token latency. The cost is slightly higher TTFT for the long request and more scheduler complexity.
explainer: Here are thirty-two chats steadily decoding, each producing one small token tick per engine step.
A huge new prompt arrives and our old scheduler prefills all of it in a single step.
That one step takes as long as hundreds of decode steps, and every chat's stream freezes.
Chunked prefill gives each step a fixed token budget, drawn as a box of fixed width.
Decodes fill the box first, one token each, and a slice of the long prompt fills the rest.
The long prompt now finishes over several steps, while the chats keep ticking at an even pace.
Since decode is memory-bound and prefill is compute-bound, sharing a step uses the hardware better too.

hook: A tiny model guesses, a big model checks, and the output distribution is exactly the big model's. Here is the proof.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — A tiny model guesses, the big model checks, and the output distribution is exactly the big model's. Not approximately. Here is the proof.

0:15 QUESTION — Decode is memory-bound, so verifying five tokens in one forward costs about the same as generating one. Leviathan et al. got 2 to 3x on T5-XXL with identical outputs. Every frontier lab serves with some form of this, and featherserve will too.

1:00 INTUITION — The draft proposes gamma tokens cheaply. The target scores all of them in one parallel pass. We keep the longest prefix the target agrees with, using a carefully designed coin flip so we never change the distribution. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Draft distribution q, target p. Sample x ~ q. Accept with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)). If rejected, sample from p'(x) = max(0, p(x) - q(x)) / sum_y max(0, p(y) - q(y)). Proof: let beta = sum_x min(p(x), q(x)), the total accept probability. P(output x) = q(x) min(1, p(x)/q(x)) + (1 - beta) p'(x) = min(p(x), q(x)) + (1 - beta) max(0, p(x) - q(x)) / (1 - beta). Note sum_y max(0, p - q) = 1 - beta, so this is min(p, q) + max(0, p - q) = p(x). Done. With per-token acceptance rate alpha and gamma drafts, expected tokens per target pass = (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / (1 - alpha). Speedup = that divided by (gamma * c + 1), where c is draft cost relative to target.

6:00 CODE — Target Qwen3-1.7B, draft Qwen3-0.6B (same tokenizer). def speculative_step(target, draft, prefix, gamma, temp): draft samples gamma tokens autoregressively saving q probs; target runs one forward on prefix plus gamma tokens getting p for gamma+1 positions; loop i: r = torch.rand(()), accept if r < p_i[x_i] / q_i[x_i]; on first reject sample from normalized clamp(p_i - q_i, min=0) and stop; if all accepted, sample a bonus token from p_{gamma+1}. Roll back draft and target KV caches to the accepted length.

9:00 RECEIPT — Distribution test on a toy vocab of 10 with fixed p and q: 200k samples from speculative_sample(p, q), chi-square test vs p, assert p-value > 0.01. Greedy test: at temperature 0, assert speculative output token-identical to target-only greedy for 50 prompts. Empirical tokens per pass within 5 percent of (1 - alpha^(gamma+1))/(1 - alpha) using measured alpha.
11:00 MEASURE — Table: gamma in 1..8 vs acceptance rate, tokens per target pass, wall-clock speedup on a 4090. Show the optimum gamma and that speedup drops on high-temperature creative prompts.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — Speculative decoding spends idle compute to skip memory-bound steps, and rejection sampling with the residual keeps it exact. Interview line: accept with min(1, p over q), resample from the normalized positive part of p minus q.
13:00 NEXT — Next: EAGLE, Medusa and friends
key_math: accept x~q w.p. min(1, p(x)/q(x)); reject -> sample p'(x) = max(0, p(x)-q(x)) / (1-beta), beta = sum_x min(p(x), q(x)); P(x) = min(p,q) + max(0,p-q) = p(x); E[tokens/pass] = (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / (1 - alpha)
code_task: speculative_sample(p[V], q[V], x) -> (accepted:bool, token); speculative_step(target, draft, prefix_ids, gamma, temperature) -> new_tokens list; KV rollback to accepted length for both models. Target Qwen3-1.7B, draft Qwen3-0.6B, RTX 4090.
receipt: scipy.stats.chisquare(counts, f_exp=200_000 * p).pvalue > 0.01 on the toy vocab; at temperature 0, spec output == target greedy output for 50 prompts; measured tokens/pass within 5% of the alpha formula.
gotchas: Using draft and target probabilities at different temperatures breaks exactness; forgetting the bonus token when all gamma are accepted loses throughput; not truncating the target's KV cache after a rejection leaves stale entries that corrupt the next step.
interview_q: Prove speculative decoding samples from the target distribution. Output probability is q(x) min(1, p/q) + (1 - beta) times the residual (p - q)+ / (1 - beta), which equals min(p, q) + (p - q)+ = p(x), since the residual mass is exactly 1 - beta.
explainer: Here are two bar charts over the same vocabulary: the draft model's guess q and the target model's p.
The draft samples a token, and we keep it with probability equal to p over q, capped at one.
Where the draft is underconfident, every guess is kept; where it overshoots the target, some guesses are rejected.
The overlap of the two bars, the minimum of p and q, is exactly the probability we accept.
On rejection we sample from what is left over: the part of p sticking above q, renormalized.
Stack the purple overlap and the blue leftover together, and the bars rebuild the target distribution exactly.
In practice the target checks five drafted tokens in one forward pass, costing about the same as one token.

hook: The best draft model is not a smaller model. It is a single layer that reads the big model's own hidden states.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — The best draft model is not a smaller model at all. It is one extra layer reading the big model's own hidden states.

0:15 QUESTION — Separate draft models need a matching tokenizer and their own KV cache, and their acceptance rates are often mediocre. EAGLE reported 2.7 to 3.5x latency speedup on LLaMA2-Chat 70B while keeping the output distribution. Medusa, EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3 and MTP heads all ship in vLLM and SGLang. Which one should featherserve support?

1:00 INTUITION — Medusa bolts several heads onto the last hidden state, each guessing token t+1, t+2, t+3 independently. EAGLE instead predicts the next hidden feature autoregressively with a small transformer layer, fed the actual sampled token, so its guesses stay consistent. Both verify with tree attention. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Medusa head k: p_k(x_{t+k} | h_t) = softmax(W_k (h_t + SiLU(U_k h_t))), independent heads, so later heads degrade quickly. EAGLE: f_{t+1} = g([f_t ; e(x_{t+1})]), then token logits = LM_head(f_{t+1}); training loss is a feature regression term plus cross-entropy on tokens. Tree verification: candidates from top-k branches form a tree; one target forward with a tree-shaped attention mask scores all paths; accept the longest path that passes. Expected accepted length tau, speedup ~ tau / (1 + draft overhead). Compare: separate draft (E09) alpha, Medusa tau, EAGLE tau.

5:30 CODE — Build tree_attention_mask(parents: list[int]) -> bool tensor [n, n] where node i sees its ancestors. Write verify_tree(target, prefix, tree_tokens, parents) using one forward with that mask and position ids = prefix_len + depth. Implement a minimal Medusa-style head on frozen Qwen3-1.7B: train 3 heads for a short run on chat data to show the idea. For EAGLE, use the published EAGLE draft checkpoint through vLLM or SGLang speculative decoding settings (see docs for exact flags) rather than training one.

9:00 RECEIPT — Tree mask unit test: assert verify_tree logits for each path equal running the target sequentially on that path (assert_close, atol=1e-2 in bf16). Then measure mean accepted length on 200 MT-Bench-style prompts for: Qwen3-0.6B draft (E09), our Medusa heads, and an EAGLE draft via the engine. Compare EAGLE's ratio to the paper's reported acceptance lengths.
11:00 MEASURE — Bar chart: accepted tokens per target forward and wall-clock speedup for each method at batch 1, then at batch 32 where spec decoding gains shrink because decode is less memory-bound.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — Draft heads beat draft models because they see the target's own features, and tree verification spends spare compute on several guesses at once. Interview line: speculative decoding helps most at low batch, where decode is most memory-bound.
13:00 NEXT — Next: Structured outputs and constrained decoding
key_math: Medusa: p_k(x_{t+k}|h_t) = softmax(W_k(h_t + SiLU(U_k h_t))); EAGLE: f_{t+1} = g([f_t ; e(x_{t+1})]), logits = W_lm f_{t+1}; tree mask M[i,j] = 1 iff j is ancestor-or-self of i; speedup ~ tau / (1 + c_draft)

gotchas: Position ids in a tree must be prefix_len + depth, not the flattened index; tree masks must combine with the causal mask over the prefix KV; spec decoding at large batch can be slower than plain decoding, so always benchmark at your real batch size.
interview_q: Why does EAGLE get higher acceptance than Medusa? Medusa heads predict each future token independently from one hidden state, while EAGLE autoregressively predicts the next feature conditioned on the sampled token, so its later guesses stay consistent with earlier ones.
explainer: Here is the target model's last hidden state, the vector that already knows a lot about what comes next.
Medusa attaches three small heads to this vector, and each head guesses one future position on its own.
Because the heads never see each other's guesses, the third head drifts and is often wrong in practice.
EAGLE instead runs a tiny layer that predicts the next hidden feature, fed the token actually sampled.
It rolls forward step by step, cheap but consistent, producing a tree of candidate continuations.
The target scores the whole tree in one forward pass, using a mask so each node only sees its ancestors.
We keep the longest branch that passes the acceptance test, often three or four tokens at once.

hook: Asking an LLM nicely for valid JSON fails sometimes. Masking the vocabulary with a grammar fails never.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Asking a model nicely for valid JSON fails sometimes. Masking its vocabulary with a grammar fails never.

0:15 QUESTION — Tool calls, agents and structured APIs from OpenAI and Anthropic need outputs that parse every single time. vLLM and SGLang implement this with XGrammar, which reported up to 100x faster mask generation than earlier approaches. We build the idea from scratch, then see why the fast version is hard.

1:00 INTUITION — At each step, some tokens would break the grammar. Set their logits to minus infinity before sampling. The model can only choose among legal continuations. The hard part is computing the legal set fast over a 150k-token vocab, every step, for every request. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Masked sampling: logits'_v = logits_v if v in Allowed(state) else -inf; p' = softmax(logits'). This is the model distribution conditioned on staying in the language, renormalized over legal tokens. A regular language is an FSM: state s, Allowed(s) = {v : delta*(s, bytes(v)) defined}. JSON with nesting needs a pushdown automaton, a stack. Precompute per FSM state is easy; for PDAs XGrammar splits tokens into context-independent (decidable from the current automaton position alone, precomputed into a bitmask cache) and context-dependent (need the stack, checked at runtime), and the second set is small.

5:00 CODE — Write a tiny JSON-schema-to-regex for {"name": string, "age": integer}. Build a character-level DFA by hand or with a small regex library. def build_token_index(dfa, vocab_strings) -> dict[state, BoolTensor[V]] by walking each token's characters from each state. def constrained_generate(model, tok, prompt, index): per step mask logits with index[state], sample, advance the DFA by the token's characters. Then compare with xgrammar's Python API or the engine's structured output option on vLLM or SGLang (see docs for the exact request fields).

8:30 RECEIPT — 1000 samples at temperature 1.0: assert all(json.loads(s) succeeds and validates against the schema) for our sampler, vs the unconstrained rate on the same prompts. Assert our mask matches the engine's: for 20 prefixes, the set of tokens our index allows equals the set xgrammar allows (or report the difference and why).
10:00 MEASURE — Table: valid-JSON rate unconstrained vs constrained; per-step mask time for our naive index vs xgrammar; end-to-end tokens/s with and without constraints in the engine.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Constrained decoding is a logit mask from an automaton, and the engineering is making that mask nearly free per step. Interview line: split the vocab into context-independent tokens you precompute and context-dependent tokens you check against the stack.
12:00 NEXT — Next: CUDA graphs for decode
key_math: logits'_v = logits_v + (0 if v in A(s) else -inf); p'(v) = p(v) 1[v in A(s)] / sum_{u in A(s)} p(u); A(s) = {v : delta*(s, bytes(v)) defined}; PDA state = (automaton node, stack)
code_task: schema_to_regex(schema) -> str; build_dfa(regex); build_token_index(dfa, vocab_strings) -> dict[int, BoolTensor[V]]; constrained_generate(model, tokenizer, prompt, index, max_tokens) -> str. Compare with xgrammar and the engine's structured-output mode.
receipt: Constrained: 1000/1000 outputs pass json.loads plus schema validation; unconstrained rate reported for contrast; allowed-token sets match xgrammar on 20 prefixes.
gotchas: Tokens span multiple characters and can cross grammar boundaries, so walk every character, not just the first; detokenization quirks like leading-space markers and byte-fallback tokens break naive string matching; forcing EOS only in accepting states, or the model stops mid-object.
interview_q: How does constrained decoding guarantee valid JSON, and what makes it slow? Each step masks logits of tokens the grammar automaton would reject, so only legal tokens can be sampled. It is slow because the legal set must be computed over the whole vocabulary per step; XGrammar precomputes context-independent tokens and checks only the few context-dependent ones at runtime.
explainer: Here is the model's probability bar chart over the vocabulary at one step of writing JSON.
Next to it is a small automaton, a set of states for what the JSON grammar allows next.
We are in the state right after an opening quote of a key, so only string characters are legal.
Every token that would break the grammar gets its bar set to zero, and the rest are rescaled.
We sample from the masked distribution, and the automaton pointer advances along every character of the chosen token.
Nested objects need a stack to remember open braces, which turns the automaton into a pushdown machine.
Most tokens can be decided without the stack, so we precompute their masks, and check only the rest live.

hook: On a small model, your GPU spends more time waiting for Python to launch kernels than running them. CUDA graphs delete that wait.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — On a small model, the GPU spends more time waiting for Python to launch kernels than running them. CUDA graphs delete that wait.

0:15 QUESTION — One decode step of Qwen3-0.6B launches hundreds of small kernels, each a few microseconds of work behind several microseconds of CPU launch overhead. vLLM, SGLang and nano-vllm all capture decode in CUDA graphs. featherserve needs it to get anywhere near them.

1:00 INTUITION — A CUDA graph is a recording. You run the decode step once while the driver records every kernel and its arguments, then replay the whole sequence with one launch. The catch: replays reuse the exact same memory addresses and shapes. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Step time without graphs ~ max(sum_k t_gpu_k, n_kernels * t_launch). With t_launch around 5 to 10 microseconds and roughly 10 to 20 kernels per layer, a 28-layer model has hundreds of launches, a few milliseconds of CPU time per step, comparable to or larger than the memory-bound GPU time of about 1.2 ms for Qwen3-0.6B. With a graph: one launch plus sum_k t_gpu_k. Shapes must be static, so capture one graph per batch-size bucket (1, 2, 4, 8, then multiples of 8 or 16), pad the batch up to the next bucket, and slice outputs.

5:00 CODE — Allocate static input buffers: input_ids[max_bs], positions[max_bs], block_tables[max_bs, max_blocks], seq_lens[max_bs], and an output logits buffer. Warm up on a side stream. For each bucket bs: g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph(); with torch.cuda.graph(g, pool=mempool): out[:bs] = model.decode(input_ids[:bs], ...). Store graphs[bs]. At runtime, copy real inputs into the static buffers with .copy_(), pick the smallest bucket >= batch, g.replay(), read out[:batch]. Mirror how nano-vllm's model_runner captures per batch size. Bonus: compare with torch.compile(mode='reduce-overhead').

8:30 RECEIPT — assert torch.equal(logits_graph[:B], logits_eager[:B]) for B in 1, 3, 17 (bitwise, same kernels). Profile with torch.profiler: eager trace shows gaps between kernels on the GPU timeline; graph trace shows them packed.
10:00 MEASURE — Decode ms per step vs batch size, eager vs CUDA graph, for Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B on the 4090. Expect the biggest win at small batch and small model, shrinking as GPU work grows.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — CUDA graphs remove CPU launch overhead by replaying a recorded step, at the price of static shapes and static memory. Interview line: graph decode, not prefill, because decode shapes are few and its kernels are tiny.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Hands-on vLLM
key_math: t_step_eager ~ max(sum_k t_gpu_k, n_launch * t_launch); t_step_graph ~ t_replay + sum_k t_gpu_k; bucket(B) = min{b in buckets : b >= B}
code_task: Static buffers input_ids[max_bs], positions[max_bs], block_tables[max_bs,max_blocks], seq_lens[max_bs], logits[max_bs,V]; capture_graphs(model, buckets) -> dict[int, CUDAGraph] via torch.cuda.CUDAGraph and torch.cuda.graph(g, pool=...); run_decode(batch) copies inputs, replays bucket graph, slices logits. Integrated in featherserve's model runner.
receipt: torch.equal(graph_logits[:B], eager_logits[:B]) for B in {1,3,17}; torch.profiler trace shows idle gaps removed; ms/step speedup reported at B=1.
gotchas: Allocating a new tensor inside the captured region or reading a Python scalar breaks capture or replays stale values; forgetting to copy_ into the static buffer replays the old inputs and silently repeats tokens; padding to a bucket must point padded slots at a dummy KV block so they do not write into real sequences.
interview_q: Why do inference engines use CUDA graphs for decode but usually not prefill? Decode launches many tiny kernels so CPU launch overhead dominates, and its shapes vary only by batch size, which buckets handle. Prefill kernels are large, so overhead is negligible, and its variable token counts make static capture awkward.
explainer: Here is a profiler timeline for one decode step, CPU row on top, GPU row underneath.
The CPU launches one kernel after another, and each launch takes a few microseconds of Python and driver work.
The GPU finishes each tiny kernel quickly, then sits idle, waiting for the next launch.
A CUDA graph records the whole sequence of kernels, with their arguments and memory addresses, once.
After that, one replay call launches the entire step, and the GPU row becomes solid with work.
Because addresses are frozen, we copy new inputs into the same static buffers before each replay.
Shapes are frozen too, so we record one graph per batch-size bucket and pad up to the nearest one.

CPU row filled with launch blocks, labels like rmsnorm, matmul, rope.
GPU row with small kernel blocks separated by white gaps.
Record icon; kernel chain collapsed into a single graph node.
Single replay arrow; GPU row now packed blocks with no gaps.

Shelf of graphs labelled bs=1,2,4,8,16,32; batch 13 padded into 16.

hook: Before you build an inference engine, run the one you are trying to beat. Here is vLLM on a 4090, with real numbers.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Before you build an inference engine, measure the one you are trying to beat. Here is vLLM on a single 4090, with real numbers.

0:15 QUESTION — featherserve's bar is 60 percent of vLLM's throughput on the same GPU and workload. That number means nothing until we have measured vLLM carefully: the right flags, the right workload, and the knobs that actually move it.

1:00 INTUITION — Every concept from this module is a vLLM flag: paged KV is gpu-memory-utilization and block size, prefix caching is a switch, chunked prefill is max-num-batched-tokens, CUDA graphs are on by default. Benchmarking is turning those knobs one at a time. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Predict before measuring. KV capacity = (0.9 * 24 GiB - weights - activations and graph memory) / kv_bytes_per_token. Qwen3-1.7B: about 3.4 GB of weights, 112 KiB per token, so roughly 150k to 160k tokens of KV, which vLLM reports in its startup log as the number of KV cache tokens or blocks. Max concurrency at 1k context is about that divided by 1024. Compare the logged number to your prediction.

4:00 CODE — On RunPod: pip install vllm. Launch: vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --max-model-len 8192 --enable-prefix-caching. Read the startup log for KV cache size and CUDA graph capture. Query with curl at /v1/completions and the openai Python client. Benchmark: vllm bench serve --model Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 256 --num-prompts 500 --request-rate 8; repeat at several rates and with infinite rate for peak throughput. Ablate one knob at a time: prefix caching on vs off, max-num-batched-tokens 2048 vs 8192, --enforce-eager to disable CUDA graphs. For speculative decoding config, see docs.

8:30 RECEIPT — Assert vLLM's logged KV capacity is within 15 percent of our predicted token count. Assert our own load generator from M13E04 and vllm bench serve agree on median TTFT within 10 percent. Record peak output tokens/s as the featherserve target.

10:00 MEASURE — Table: config vs throughput, TTFT p50/p99, ITL p99. Plots: throughput and p99 TTFT vs request rate; effect of enforce-eager at low concurrency; effect of max-num-batched-tokens on ITL tail.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — vLLM is this module's ideas behind flags, and the baseline must be measured at a stated rate, length distribution and config. Interview line: report throughput at an SLO, not at infinite request rate alone.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Hands-on SGLang
key_math: KV_tokens ~ (util * M_gpu - M_weights - M_act) / kv_bytes_per_token; Qwen3-1.7B: (0.9*24 GiB - ~3.4 GB - overhead) / 112 KiB ~ 1.5e5 tokens; max_concurrency ~ KV_tokens / context_len

receipt: Logged KV cache tokens within 15% of predict_kv_capacity(); our load generator and vllm bench serve agree on median TTFT within 10%; peak tokens/s recorded as the featherserve baseline.
gotchas: Benchmarking with the client on a different machine adds network latency to TTFT, so run it on the pod; the first requests include warmup, discard them; random datasets with prefix caching on give no hits, so use a shared-prefix workload to see caching.
interview_q: How would you benchmark an inference server fairly? Fix model, GPU, precision and workload distribution, sweep request rate with open-loop arrivals, report throughput alongside TTFT and ITL percentiles at a stated SLO, and ablate one configuration knob at a time.
explainer: Here is the vLLM server as a box, with each idea from this module drawn as a dial on its front panel.
The memory dial sets how much of the GPU goes to the paged KV cache after the weights load.
We predict the cache size from our formula, then check it against the number vLLM prints at startup.
The batched tokens dial is the chunked prefill budget, trading first-token latency for smooth streaming.
The prefix caching switch only matters when prompts share a prefix, so random prompts show nothing.
We sweep the request rate, and plot throughput rising while tail latency eventually takes off.
The point where tail latency crosses our SLO is the honest number featherserve has to chase.

hook: Same model, same GPU, same prompts. On a shared-prefix workload, the engine with a radix tree pulls far ahead. Let us measure it.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Same model, same GPU, same prompts. On a shared-prefix workload, the engine built around a radix tree pulls ahead. Let us measure by how much.

0:15 QUESTION — SGLang powers serving at xAI and many others and is the reference for RadixAttention. Agents, few-shot evals and multi-turn chat all reuse prefixes. featherserve's radix cache came from SGLang's design, so we compare against it head to head.

1:00 INTUITION — SGLang has two halves. The runtime: a scheduler with a radix cache, chunked prefill, overlap scheduling and CUDA graphs. The frontend: a Python language where fork and gen calls express branching programs, which the runtime turns into prefix hits. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Shared-prefix workload: G groups, each with a system prompt of length P_s, and Q questions per group of length P_q, output length O. Ideal prefill tokens with caching = G*P_s + G*Q*P_q vs no caching G*Q*(P_s + P_q). Ideal hit rate = (Q-1) P_s / (Q (P_s + P_q)). With P_s=2048, P_q=128, Q=32, that is about 91 percent, so prefill work drops by roughly 10x. Throughput gain is smaller because decode is unchanged; predict it from the prefill fraction of total time.

4:30 CODE — Launch: python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B --port 30000. Benchmark: python -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --dataset-name generated-shared-prefix (group and length options: see docs). Repeat with --disable-radix-cache. Try --schedule-policy lpm vs fcfs. Run vLLM with --enable-prefix-caching on the same workload using our load generator. Frontend: @sgl.function def multi_q(s, doc, qs): s += doc; forks = s.fork(len(qs)); for f, q in zip(forks, qs): f += q + sgl.gen('a', max_tokens=128). Set the backend with sgl.set_default_backend(sgl.RuntimeEndpoint('http://localhost:30000')).

8:30 RECEIPT — Read the cache hit rate from SGLang's server log and assert it is within 5 points of our predicted 91 percent. Assert throughput with radix cache over without is above 2x on this workload, and record SGLang vs vLLM prefix caching on identical prompts.
10:00 MEASURE — Table: engine and config vs throughput, TTFT p50/p99, hit rate: SGLang radix on/off, lpm vs fcfs, vLLM prefix caching on/off. Plot TTFT CDF for all four.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Prefix reuse is a workload property, and engines designed around it win big exactly when prompts share structure. Interview line: longest-prefix-match scheduling raises hit rate by running requests that share cached prefixes together.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Build a mini inference engine
key_math: prefill_cached = G*P_s + G*Q*P_q; prefill_nocache = G*Q*(P_s + P_q); hit_ideal = (Q-1)*P_s / (Q*(P_s+P_q)); P_s=2048, P_q=128, Q=32 -> ~0.91
code_task: Launch SGLang and vLLM servers; run sglang.bench_serving with generated-shared-prefix and our own load generator on identical prompts; predict_hit_rate(G, Q, P_s, P_q); SGLang frontend program with @sgl.function, s.fork, sgl.gen against sgl.RuntimeEndpoint.
receipt: Logged hit rate within 5 points of predict_hit_rate(); radix-on / radix-off throughput > 2x on the shared-prefix workload; SGLang vs vLLM numbers on identical prompts recorded.
gotchas: Comparing engines with different max context or memory fractions is unfair, so match them; requests arriving all at once before the first prefix is cached get no hits, so warm one request per group or use lpm; frontend fork only shares KV if branches run on the same server.
interview_q: When does RadixAttention help a lot and when not at all? It helps when many requests share long prefixes, like system prompts, few-shot examples, multi-turn history or tree search. With unique prompts there are no hits and it adds only a little overhead.

Without a prefix cache, the server prefills that same long document thirty-two separate times, one tall bar each.
SGLang's radix tree stores the document once, and every later question walks straight down that branch.
Our formula predicts about ninety one percent of prompt tokens hit the cache for this workload.
Longest-prefix-match scheduling reorders the queue so requests with cached prefixes run together, and the branch stays warm.
The frontend's fork call writes this pattern directly in Python: one shared document, then many parallel generations.
We compare both engines on identical prompts, and the TTFT curves separate exactly where hits occur.

hook: nano-vllm matches vLLM's offline throughput in about twelve hundred lines of Python. We read it, then write our own.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — nano-vllm gets close to vLLM's offline throughput in about twelve hundred lines of Python. We read it, then we put ours next to it.

0:15 QUESTION — vLLM and SGLang are hundreds of thousands of lines. nano-vllm and mini-sglang distill them into code one person can read in an evening. This episode assembles featherserve from the parts built in E05 to E12 and measures the gap to vLLM. The bar is 60 percent.

1:00 INTUITION — Every engine is the same loop: scheduler picks a batch, block manager finds memory, model runner executes with CUDA graphs, sampler picks tokens, sequences update. nano-vllm makes that loop visible. mini-sglang adds the radix cache and overlap scheduling, where the CPU plans the next batch while the GPU runs the current one. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Where the gap comes from, as a budget per decode step: t = t_sched (Python) + t_prepare (building input tensors and block tables) + t_gpu. If t_sched + t_prepare is 2 ms and t_gpu is 4 ms, overlap scheduling hides the 2 ms and gives 1.5x. Kernel gap: attention over paged KV in PyTorch gather vs a fused paged attention kernel such as FlashInfer or FlashAttention varlen with block tables. Throughput target: 0.6 * vLLM tokens/s from M13E13.

4:30 CODE — Walkthrough, on screen: nano-vllm's llm_engine (step loop), scheduler (prefill-first then decode, preemption), block_manager (block allocation and hash-based prefix caching), model_runner (tensor prep, CUDA graph capture per batch size), sequence (state). Then mini-sglang: radix cache, chunked prefill, overlap scheduling; describe their roles rather than line numbers. Then featherserve: assemble Engine(model, scheduler, block_manager, radix_cache, runner, sampler), an OpenAI-compatible /v1/completions with FastAPI and streaming, and swap our gather attention for a fused paged attention kernel from a library where available.

8:30 RECEIPT — Greedy outputs from featherserve equal HF transformers greedy for 50 prompts. Offline throughput on the same 500 random prompts (1024 in, 256 out) for featherserve, nano-vllm and vLLM; assert featherserve >= 0.6 * vLLM, or show the profiler breakdown that explains the miss.
10:00 MEASURE — Table: tokens/s, TTFT p50/p99, ITL p99 for featherserve, nano-vllm, vLLM, SGLang. Flame graph of one featherserve step with CPU and GPU time labelled, and the top three gaps to vLLM.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — A real engine is a small loop around four data structures, and the last factor of two is CPU overhead and kernels. Interview line: overlap scheduling hides CPU planning behind GPU execution.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Disaggregated prefill/decode and TP serving

interview_q: Walk me through the main loop of an inference engine. The scheduler picks running decodes and prefill chunks under a token budget, the block manager allocates KV blocks and reuses cached prefixes, the model runner builds inputs and runs the model with CUDA graphs for decode, the sampler picks tokens, and finished sequences free their blocks.
explainer: Here is the engine loop as four boxes in a circle: scheduler, block manager, model runner, sampler.
The scheduler pulls waiting requests and running ones into a batch under a fixed token budget.
The block manager hands out KV blocks, reusing any prefix blocks already in the cache.
The model runner packs inputs into static buffers and replays a CUDA graph for the decode part.
The sampler picks one token per sequence, and finished sequences give their blocks back to the free list.
In a naive engine, the GPU timeline shows idle gaps while Python on the CPU plans the next step.
Overlap scheduling plans step two on the CPU while the GPU runs step one, closing most of that gap.

hook: Prefill wants compute, decode wants bandwidth, and putting them on the same GPU makes both worse. So big deployments split them.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Prefill wants compute, decode wants bandwidth, and sharing one GPU makes both worse. So the biggest deployments split them onto different machines.

0:15 QUESTION — DistServe reported serving 7.4x more requests or meeting 12.6x tighter SLOs by disaggregating prefill and decode. DeepSeek, Kimi and others serve with prefill-decode disaggregation, and SGLang and vLLM both support it. When does it pay off, and when is chunked prefill on one box enough?

1:00 INTUITION — Two kitchens: one only does prep, one only plates. Prep stations are sized for heavy work, plating for speed. The cost is carrying each dish between kitchens, here the KV cache over the network. Tensor parallelism is the other axis: split each layer across GPUs to fit bigger models and get more bandwidth per token. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — KV transfer per request = P * kv_bytes_per_token. Qwen3-1.7B, P=4096: 4096 * 112 KiB = 448 MiB. Llama-3-8B: 4096 * 128 KiB = 512 MiB. At 50 GB/s effective (RDMA or NVLink class) that is about 10 ms; at 10 Gb/s Ethernet (1.25 GB/s) it is about 0.4 s. Disaggregation pays when transfer time << prefill time and interference cost is large. Capacity planning: choose prefill GPUs n_p and decode GPUs n_d so lambda * t_prefill / n_p meets the TTFT SLO and decode batch per GPU meets the TPOT SLO. TP serving: per-token weight bytes per GPU fall by the TP degree t, so ideal decode latency falls by t, minus two all-reduces per layer of size B * d * bytes.

5:30 CODE — Mac only, no GPUs needed. Write cost_model(P, O, lambda, slo_ttft, slo_tpot, model_cfg, gpu, link_bw) that returns, for colocated with chunked prefill vs disaggregated (n_p, n_d), the predicted goodput per GPU using the step-time models from E03 and E08 and the transfer time above. Sweep link bandwidth and prompt length. Draw the architecture: router, prefill pool, KV transfer, decode pool. For real systems, show SGLang's and vLLM's disaggregation docs and their transfer backends (see docs; no flags invented).

8:30 RECEIPT — Sanity-check the cost model against a published point: plug DistServe's setting in qualitatively and confirm disaggregation wins when SLOs are tight and links are fast, and loses on slow links or short prompts. Assert KV transfer size matches 2 * L * n_kv * d_head * bytes * P exactly in code.

10:00 MEASURE — Heatmap: prompt length x link bandwidth, colour = goodput ratio disaggregated over colocated. Mark the break-even contour. Second plot: TP degree vs ideal decode latency with and without all-reduce cost.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Disaggregation removes prefill-decode interference at the cost of moving KV, so it wins with long prompts, tight SLOs and fast interconnects. Interview line: compute KV transfer bytes per request before proposing disaggregation.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Evals 101
key_math: KV_transfer = P * 2 * L * n_kv * d_head * bytes; t_transfer = KV_transfer / link_bw; pay-off if t_transfer << t_prefill and interference penalty large; TP decode: t ~ 2N/(t_deg * BW) + 2 * L * allreduce(B*d*bytes)
code_task: cost_model(P, O, lam, slo_ttft, slo_tpot, cfg, gpu, link_bw) -> {colocated_goodput_per_gpu, disagg_goodput_per_gpu, best_np_nd}; kv_transfer_bytes(cfg, P); sweep and heatmap; architecture diagram of router, prefill pool, KV transfer, decode pool.
receipt: kv_transfer_bytes(Qwen3-1.7B, 4096) == 4096 * 2 * 28 * 8 * 128 * 2 (469,762,048 bytes); cost model reproduces the qualitative DistServe result: disaggregation wins at tight SLOs with fast links, loses on slow links or short prompts.
gotchas: Forgetting GQA and using n_heads instead of n_kv overstates transfer by the group factor; treating chunked prefill as zero-interference makes colocated look too good or too bad, model it with the E08 step time; TP all-reduce latency at small batch is latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound.
interview_q: When would you disaggregate prefill and decode? When long prompts and tight TTFT and TPOT SLOs make interference costly, and the interconnect moves the KV cache quickly relative to prefill time; with short prompts or slow links, colocated serving with chunked prefill is usually better.
explainer: Here is one GPU juggling both phases, long prefill blocks interrupting a stream of small decode steps.
Every prefill delays decodes, and every decode batch slows prefills, so both latency targets suffer.
Disaggregation gives prefill its own pool of GPUs and decode its own pool, each tuned for its roofline.
After prefill, the request's KV cache travels across the network to a decode GPU, drawn as a moving block.
We size that block with our formula, about four hundred fifty mebibytes for a four thousand token prompt.
On a fast link it arrives in milliseconds, on slow Ethernet it takes longer than the prefill itself.
The heatmap shows where splitting pays: long prompts, tight targets, and fast links in the top corner.
